claim: The web token set is a wholly different brand from the Android design system: web brand is marigold #E2A04A on near-black warm ink #0E0B08, while the Android palette is deep-green primary #0B3D2E on cream #FBF7EF. There is no green primary anywhere in globals.css.
Radius scales diverge by ~2x: web sm/md/lg = 2/4/6px, Android sm/md/lg/xl = 4/8/12/20dp. A card in the admin console and a card in the customer app cannot look like the same product.

Motion durations diverge: web fast/base/slow = 120/220/420ms, Android fast/base/medium/slow = 150/200/300/500ms. Easing curves DO align (web --ease-out == Android emphasizedDecelerate; web --ease-in-out == Android standard).
Web adds a serif display face (Fraunces) that has no counterpart in the Android type system, so the brand's headline voice exists on web only.
Web spacing scale introduces a 2px step (--space-0-5) and a 20px step (--space-5) that are off the Android 4px/8px token grid, so 'the same gap' is unreproducible across platforms.

Semantic status colours diverge from Android: web success #5BA38E / warn #E9B44C / danger #B6385C vs Android success #10A85E / warning #EBA53A / error #D73C3C. An 'error' badge is a different hue on each platform.
The stylesheet emits no .empty-state rule despite EmptyState.tsx tagging every empty state with that class — the hook for a shared empty-state visual language exists but is unimplemented.
The .eyebrow and .chip primitives apply uppercase + wide tracking with no :lang(hi) reset, while nav labels and table cells do get one — inconsistent Devanagari handling.

DESIGN.md is still the untouched scaffold template — every token value is a '#...' or '<family>' placeholder — while a fully-specified 653-line token system ships in globals.css. There is no written design contract for the shipped design.
The document's stated motion default (200ms) contradicts the implemented --duration-base (220ms), so the only concrete number in the doc is already wrong.

The doc's own anti-pattern list forbids 'generic rounded-card' aesthetics; the dashboard widgets are exactly flat 1px-bordered rectangles with no elevation or imagery, which is the opposite failure mode and is not covered.
No skip-link is rendered before the Rail, so every keyboard/screen-reader user traverses 10 nav links before reaching page content.

Four font families are loaded on every route (Fraunces with 4 weights + italics, Geist, JetBrains Mono, Noto Devanagari) — a heavy payload for a rural-UP audience on 3G, and Fraunces italic is used by exactly one helper class.
The meta description is a hardcoded English literal while every other metadata string is translated.
No app icon asset exists — public/ contains only firebase-messaging-sw.js and robots.txt, and app/ has no icon.* file.
There is no marketing/landing surface at all — the bare origin goes straight to a login form, so the product has no first impression for anyone who is not already an admin.
This route correctly derives the locale from routing.defaultLocale, unlike app/not-found.tsx:21 which hardcodes /hi/dashboard.

Every string on this 404 is a hardcoded English literal even though the exact translations already exist in messages/hi.json under the 'notFound' namespace and are used by the sibling [locale]/not-found.tsx.
The CTA hardcodes /hi/dashboard, so an English admin who hits a root 404 is bounced into the Hindi console.
lang="en" is forced on the <main>, which would disable Devanagari shaping rules for any Hindi content rendered inside this boundary.

The global error screen re-implements the entire design system as inline hex literals (9 raw colours, 7 raw sizes) and uses system-ui instead of the brand fonts, so the app's worst-case screen is the one that looks least like the product.
#2A251E is used as the card border but is not a token anywhere in globals.css — it is an invented value that will drift from --ink-4 (#2E2719) forever.
The incident-reference text uses #6E665B, the exact colour globals.css:24 documents as a 3.33:1 AA failure that was already remediated everywhere else.
The document is hardcoded lang="hi" while its content is 90% English, and its one Hindi phrase contradicts the translated globalError.title already in messages/hi.json.
Because it is inline-styled with dark hex values, this screen ignores the light-theme override entirely — a light-mode admin gets a black crash screen.
The Reload button has no hover, focus or active styling and no border-radius, unlike every other button in the app.
The whole message catalogue is shipped to the client on every localized route via NextIntlClientProvider with no namespace narrowing — a payload cost on rural 3G.
Redirects an already-authenticated admin to /login rather than /dashboard — there is no session check here, so the logged-in landing experience depends entirely on the login page's own refresh probe.
Raw Firebase exception messages are rendered directly into the user-facing error banner in five separate code paths, so an admin can see strings like 'Firebase: Error (auth/network-request-failed).'

The login page has no language switcher. LocaleSwitcher is mounted only inside the authenticated dashboard layout, so a Hindi-preferring admin landing on /en/login (or an English admin on the /hi default) cannot change language before signing in.

'Continue with Google' renders as a bare marigold text button with no Google mark, while the email/password submit is a ghost button — the OAuth affordance is unrecognisable and looks like a generic primary CTA.
Loading is communicated only by swapping button text; there is no spinner, progress bar or skeleton anywhere on the sign-in flow, so a slow rural connection reads as a frozen page.
No password-visibility toggle, no 'forgot password' link and no caps-lock hint on the password field.
Two spacing systems are mixed inside one component — arbitrary CSS-var utilities (gap-[var(--space-5)], line 349) alongside Tailwind's default numeric scale (gap-2 line 381, gap-3 line 427).
The step-1 → step-2 swap replaces the entire form body with no transition or focus move, so after a successful password the OTP field is not focused and the change is not announced.
The left panel is a flat single-colour rectangle carrying only text — no imagery, pattern, product screenshot or brand mark on the single most-seen unauthenticated screen.
The entire setup screen is untranslated English — the file never imports next-intl — on a product whose default locale is Hindi.
Every failure path in the init effect silently router.replace('/login') with no message, so an admin whose network blips during enrolment is dumped back at sign-in with no explanation.
All four redirects use unprefixed paths ('/login', '/dashboard') inside a localePrefix:'always' routing config, so they do not preserve the user's locale segment.

The setup card duplicates the login card's layout with drifted values — 58rem vs 64rem max-width, 3.3rem vs 3.5rem headline clamp, 25rem vs 26rem measure — so two consecutive screens in one flow do not line up.
The QR loading affordance is a bare grey animate-pulse square that bypasses the project's own .skeleton shimmer primitive.
Successful MFA enrolment produces no confirmation — the user is pushed straight to /dashboard with no 'you're protected' moment on a security-critical action.
The authenticated shell has no sign-out control. `logout` is implemented in the auth context but is never called from any component in the app.

claim: The shell shows no signed-in identity — no name, email, role badge or avatar anywhere in Topbar or Rail — despite the layout already holding adminId and role in initialAuth.
A role that fails normalizeAdminRole is redirected to /login instead of the purpose-built not-authorized page, so the RBAC explanation screen is unreachable from the shell.
No route-transition feedback of any kind — no top progress bar, no pending state on Rail links — on an app whose pages are server components doing network fetches.
The shell is written entirely in inline style objects while its own children use Tailwind arbitrary values and global CSS classes — a third styling paradigm in one file.

The flagship Live Ops dashboard has no loading state at all — no loading.tsx sibling exists, unlike orders, finance, complaints, audit-log and technicians which all ship one — so it renders blank while two API calls resolve.
The entire dashboard is untranslated English served under the default Hindi locale — there is no 'dashboard' namespace in either message catalogue.
The page has no <h1>; the highest heading is <h2> inside widgets and the page title lives in a Topbar <span>, so heading hierarchy starts at level 2 with nothing above it.

Two dead className hooks are applied to the grids — 'dashboard-grid-feed' and 'dashboard-grid-payout' have no rule anywhere in globals.css, so the intended per-row responsive behaviour does not exist; only the generic .dashboard-grid single-column collapse fires below 900px.
The right-hand columns of the two rows are different widths (340px then 280px), so the dashboard's right edge steps inward halfway down the page.
A malformed API response throws a developer sentence into the user-facing error boundary rather than a handled empty/degraded state.
The 401 and 403 redirects omit the locale prefix under a localePrefix:'always' config.
Every spacing value on the page is a raw literal (1.25rem, 1400px, 340px, 280px) with no --space-* token in the file.
When no `next` param is present — the normal case for a middleware 403 — the page renders with no action at all: no link back, no contact-owner path, no sign-out. It is a dead end.
Fully untranslated English on an RBAC screen that a Hindi-speaking operator is most likely to hit.
The card uses --radius-md while every other centred card in the cluster is square-cornered, and its background equals the page background so it reads as an unstyled block.
Vertical centring uses calc(100vh - 72px) but the Topbar is 52px tall, so the card sits 20px off centre.
A raw URL path is interpolated into an English sentence, which is both unlocalisable and exposes internal routing to the user.
Every Topbar string is hardcoded English while fully-translated Hindi equivalents already exist unused in messages/hi.json under the 'topbar' namespace.
The 'LIVE' indicator is hardcoded and unconditional — it pulses regardless of connection or data freshness, so it is a false status signal on an operations console.
The product name is rendered in --color-text-muted, making the brand the dimmest text in the header while a 24px ticking clock sits beside it — the hierarchy is inverted.
The clock is empty on first paint and then appears, reflowing the right-hand group; there is no reserved-width placeholder.
The city name comes from an env var with an 'Ayodhya' literal fallback baked into the client bundle, so a mis-set env silently ships the wrong city into the header.
The header contains no search, no notifications, no account menu and no breadcrumb — an operations console topbar with only a clock.
`outline: 'none'` is applied inline to every desktop nav link, which defeats the global :focus-visible ring and leaves the primary navigation with no visible keyboard focus indicator.

The mobile bottom bar renders only the first five nav items with no overflow or 'More' affordance, so up to five capability-granted sections (audit log, admin users, compliance, technicians, customers for a super-admin) are unreachable below 900px.
The brand mark is a placeholder — a teal square with the letters 'HS' — on a product named HomeHeroo, and it is aria-hidden so it carries no accessible brand identity either.

Ten navigation items are rendered as one flat undifferentiated list with 2px gaps — no sections, no dividers, no grouping between operational (Live Ops, Orders) and governance (Audit Log, Compliance) areas.
Every dimension in the Rail is a raw literal — 192px, 12px, 10px, 0.8125rem, 0.68rem — with no --space-* or --text-* token used anywhere in the file.
Both desktop (~34px) and mobile (~40px) nav targets fall below the 44px minimum touch target.
A role whose capability set yields no nav items renders a completely blank rail with no message or fallback.
The rail cannot be collapsed and has no icon-only mode, permanently consuming 192px on a data-dense operations console.
Textbook flat-gray-card syndrome: six identical --ink-2 rectangles with a 1px border, 2px radius, no icon, no trend, no delta, no sparkline — differentiated only by the hue of the numeral.
All six KPI labels are hardcoded English with no i18n namespace, including the untranslated finance jargon 'GMV'.

Currency formatting hardcodes the 'en-IN' locale and sets no fraction-digit policy, so a paise value that is not a whole rupee renders with a ragged single decimal place and breaks numeric alignment across tiles.
Tile labels at 11px in --fog-0 sit on --ink-2, a lighter background than the --ink-1 the token's 4.54:1 measurement was taken against, so they fall below AA.
There is no loading, empty or stale state — a zero-data day and a failed refresh look identical to a real zero.
Revenue-sensitive figures (GMV, commission, pending payouts) render for every role with no capability gate, while the far less sensitive payout CTA is gated behind finance.read.
Every dimension is a raw literal that shadows an existing token (0.6875rem = --text-eyebrow, 1.5rem = --text-2xl), so the tiles will not follow a future scale change.

There is no loading state — before the first poll resolves the component renders the 'The feed is quiet' empty state, actively telling the operator there is no activity when the data has simply not arrived.
Event kind is communicated by a 3px border colour alone with no icon or text label, so alerts and completions are indistinguishable to a colour-blind operator.
New events appear with no motion, no highlight and no unread affordance on a 30-second poll cycle — the 'live' feed has no liveness.
The error card has no retry action; recovery requires waiting a full 30-second poll or reloading the page.
All feed chrome is hardcoded English on the Hindi-default dashboard.
aria-live="polite" is set on the entire 50-item list rather than on newly-added rows, so each poll risks re-announcing the whole feed.
Timestamps render at 10px in the faintest text colour — effectively unreadable at normal viewing distance.
Feed rows are not clickable — there is no route from an event to the underlying order, technician or complaint.
The largest widget on the flagship dashboard is not a map — it is seven 12%-opacity straight lines with coloured dots on top, with no basemap, roads, landmarks or city outline.

claim: The legend plate uses a hardcoded blue-grey rgba(14,20,22,0.85) that is neither a token nor part of the warm-ink palette, and it does not respond to the light theme — in light mode dark --fog-1 text sits on a dark plate.
Pins are non-interactive 10px dots (cursor:'default'), so an operator cannot click, hover or tap a technician to see who they are or what they are on — the map is decorative.

The bounding box is hardcoded to a ~10km Ayodhya window; any technician outside it computes a percentage below 0 or above 100 and is clipped by overflow:hidden, silently disappearing from the operations view.
The empty state is wrapped in pointer-events:none, permanently disabling any action the shared EmptyState component might render.
Legend and empty-state copy are hardcoded English, and the legend is a fixed-width no-wrap row that will overflow with longer Hindi labels.
The 'idle' state uses --fog-0, the body-text token, making idle pins nearly indistinguishable from the background grid.
Unlike every sibling widget, the map has no h2 heading — only an aria-label — so it is unlabeled visually.
Currency is rendered as 'INR 1,234' here while the KPI tile directly above renders '₹1,234' for the same paise value — two currency conventions on one screen.

The primary call-to-action is styled as a low-contrast grey box — --fog-0 text on --ink-3 — with no hover, focus or active state, so the money action on the dashboard is the least prominent element in its own card.

The empty state is bespoke small italic faint text rather than the shared EmptyState component, giving the dashboard three different empty-state treatments (EmptyState card in OrderFeed, EmptyState overlay in TechMap, italic line here).
All nine strings including the payout schedule are hardcoded English on the Hindi-default dashboard.
The payout schedule 'Weekly - Sun 23:59 IST' is a hardcoded string, not derived from configuration, so it will silently lie if the schedule changes.
Copy uses ASCII hyphens as sentence dashes ('Nothing pending - payouts cleared.', 'Weekly - Sun') while the rest of the product uses proper en/em dashes and middots.

The utilisation chart renders 24 hardcoded fake percentages as if they were live operational data, with no 'sample data' label, no disabled styling and no empty state — an operations console presenting fiction as fact.
The dashboard page renders <UtilStrip /> with no props at all, so the seed fallback is guaranteed to be what ships.
Data values are reachable only through a native `title` tooltip, so keyboard, touch and screen-reader users can never read a single number from the chart.
Axis labels are 9px — the smallest type in the application and roughly half the body size — rendered in the faintest text token.
The widget uses a 6px container radius while every sibling dashboard widget uses --radius-sm (2px), so one card in the row has visibly rounder corners than the rest.
The colour semantics are inverted: >75% utilisation is painted --coral, the same alarm colour used for open complaints, so a highly productive workforce reads as an incident.
The chart uses 12-hour am/pm labels while the Topbar clock on the same screen uses 24-hour time.
A 48px-tall chart occupies a full grid column beside a 340px feed, leaving a large band of dead space in the second dashboard row.

There is no 'system' / 'auto' theme option — DEFAULT_THEME is hardcoded to 'dark' in src/lib/theme.ts and prefers-color-scheme is never consulted, so a first-time visitor on a light-configured OS gets a near-black console.
A failed cookie write is silently swallowed, so a user whose preference does not persist gets no feedback and will re-toggle on every page load.
The theme flip is instantaneous with no colour transition on html/body, so switching light↔dark is a hard strobe across the full viewport.
The toggle's hit area is roughly 13px tall — 11px text with zero vertical padding — making it one of the smallest interactive targets in the product.
Two adjacent controls in the same Topbar slot implement radiogroup semantics differently — LocaleSwitcher has roving tabindex and arrow-key navigation, ThemeToggle has neither.
'Dark' and 'Light' are hardcoded English with no theme namespace in either message catalogue.
The two controls sitting side by side are also visually inconsistent — LocaleSwitcher is a bordered segmented pill track, ThemeToggle is naked underlined text.
The component emits className="empty-state" but no such rule exists anywhere in globals.css, so the shared class hook is dead and all styling is inline.

The props interface has no icon or illustration slot, guaranteeing that every empty state across the product is a text-only dashed box — the single largest contributor to the 'unfinished' feel of the console.
There is no severity or variant prop, so OrderFeed uses the identical treatment for a benign empty feed and a hard API failure.
The `action` slot exists but no caller in this cluster passes one, and TechMap wraps the component in pointer-events:none so an action would be unclickable there anyway.
A dashed border is a wireframe convention that reads as unfinished UI in a production console.

The app has two competing button systems: this React component and the .btn/.btn-primary/.btn-ghost CSS classes. Every real screen uses the CSS classes; the React component is imported only by its own test file, so the 'shared primitive' is dead code.

The two systems disagree on fundamentals — radius 4px here vs 2px in .btn, no min-height here vs 44px in .btn, no uppercase/tracking here vs uppercase 0.04em in .btn — so adopting the component would visibly change every button.
The component defines no hover, active or pressed styling at all — only a disabled opacity — so it provides no micro-interaction feedback.
No loading state and no icon slot, despite both being required by the login and setup flows (which is likely why those screens fell back to raw .btn classes plus manual text swaps).
The ghost variant has a transparent background AND a transparent border, so at rest it is indistinguishable from plain text.
Page metadata title is a hardcoded English literal while the sibling audit-log route localizes its metadata via getTranslations — inconsistent i18n discipline across the same route group.
No route-level error.tsx in orders/; only loading.tsx and page.tsx exist in the directory.

Loading skeleton does not mirror the real Orders layout — one h-10 bar substitutes for an 8-control filter row and 8 identical h-12 bars substitute for a 9-column table with a header band and pagination footer, so the layout visibly jumps on hydration.

This route-level skeleton is dead weight for the actual data fetch: OrdersClient fetches orders client-side in useEffect and renders nothing at all while data is null, so operators see a blank content area after the skeleton disappears.
Skeleton uses raw Tailwind spacing (p-6, space-y-3) rather than the globals.css --space-* token scale used elsewhere in the same route group.
No role="status" / aria-busy on the loading region, so assistive tech gets no load announcement.

There is no loading state for the orders fetch — the table is conditionally rendered only when data is non-null, so first paint and every filter/pagination change blanks the content region with no skeleton or spinner.
The table's isLoading prop is hardcoded to false and then discarded by the table (`void isLoading`), so the loading affordance is wired up but permanently dead.
Error surface prints the raw exception via String(e) rather than a written, translated operator message, and offers no retry affordance.
The error paragraph lacks role="alert"/aria-live, so a fetch failure is silent for screen-reader operators (contrast with CustomerListClient which does set role="alert").
CSV export failure is swallowed: handleExport has try/finally with no catch, so a failed fetchAllOrdersForExport rejects unhandled and the operator only sees the button stop spinning.
Export button gives no progress feedback beyond a text swap — no spinner, no row count, no aria-live, on an operation that pages through the full result set.
updateUrl force-resets page to 1 on every patch including the pagination patch path, but pagination calls updateUrl({page:p}) — the spread order means `page: 1` overrides the requested page.
router.replace targets a locale-less '/orders?...' path, discarding the [locale] segment on every filter change.

Table rows are not keyboard operable — <tr onClick> with no tabIndex/role/onKeyDown means opening an order detail is impossible without a mouse, and the 'View' affordance in the last column is inert text, not a button or link.

The currency column does not use the tabular-nums helper that globals.css:280 defines (.tnum), and is left-aligned, so rupee amounts misalign down the column — a Stripe-bar table failure. CustomerCell and TechnicianCell do apply tabular-nums to IDs/phones, making the omission on the money column inconsistent as well.
The header row is not sticky — on a 50-row page (pageSize 50, set in OrdersClient.tsx:37) column headers scroll out of view with no re-anchoring.
No bulk selection: there is no checkbox column, no select-all, and no bulk action bar anywhere in the table, so every override is one order at a time.
No column sorting at all — no aria-sort, no sortable headers, and OrdersQueryParams usage in OrdersClient never sets a sort key.
isLoading is accepted then discarded via `void isLoading`, so the table cannot show a refetch/stale state.
The pagination summary string '{total} total · page {page} of {totalPages}' is hardcoded English inside an otherwise fully translated component, in a Hindi-default product.
Pagination aria-labels 'Previous page' and 'Next page' are hardcoded English while their visible labels are translated — screen-reader Hindi users get English.
Order IDs are truncated to 8 characters with no tooltip, no title attribute, and no copy affordance, so an operator cannot retrieve the full ID from the list view.
No <th scope="col"> and no <caption>, so the table is unlabelled for screen readers; the sibling AuditLogTable does set scope, proving the inconsistency is unintentional.
Nine columns inside overflow-x-auto with no column priority, no responsive hiding, and no min-width per column — the table simply scrolls sideways on narrower viewports.
Row hover has no transition duration, so the highlight snaps rather than easing at the 120ms token globals.css:174 defines.

The slide-over has NO enter/exit animation — no transform, transition, or duration anywhere in the file; it is a hard mount/unmount of a fixed panel, which is exactly the jarring choreography the Linear/Stripe bar rules out.

The panel background is literal bg-white with Tailwind gray text on a dark-default editorial admin theme, so it ignores the design system entirely and produces a full-height white slab over a #0E0B08 dashboard.

Ten distinct raw Tailwind palette colours (gray-800/500/400/700/200/50, black/30, white) appear in this one file, none of which are globals.css tokens and none of which respond to the light/dark theme switch.
Evidence-photo stage labels are a hardcoded English lookup with an enum-underscore fallback, shipping English operational vocabulary into a Hindi-first console.
Evidence photos have no loading placeholder, no error/broken-image fallback, and no lightbox — clicking opens the raw storage URL in a new tab, dumping the operator out of the console.

The toast is rendered inline in the scrollable body rather than pinned, and never auto-dismisses, so an override confirmation can appear off-screen above the action buttons the operator is looking at.
The detail fetch failure is silently swallowed, so the panel can show stale list-row data indefinitely with no staleness indicator.
Image alt text is a hardcoded English template string, so the only description of evidence photos for a screen-reader operator is untranslated.
The close control is a bare '×' character with leading-none and no padding, giving roughly a 20px hit target.
Eight consecutive identically-styled label/value sections with no grouping, dividers, or visual hierarchy make the detail panel read as a form dump rather than a designed record.
Panel width is a hardcoded max-w-md with no resize/expand affordance, on a surface that also hosts a photo grid and a 6-button override panel.
Six of eight filter controls have no visible or programmatic label — they rely entirely on placeholders, which vanish once a value is entered, leaving unlabeled boxes.

Text filters fire onChange on every keystroke and OrdersClient immediately rewrites the URL and refetches — there is no debounce, no submit, and no Enter-to-apply, so typing a 10-digit phone number issues ten network requests and ten history replacements.
No 'clear filters' affordance and no active-filter count anywhere in the row, so an operator cannot tell why the table is empty or reset in one action.
The amount filters give no currency unit — no ₹ affix, no helper text — while the table formats paise divided by 100, so the operator has no way to know the expected input scale.
Date-range aria-labels are hardcoded English ('Date from'/'Date to') in a Hindi-default product.

Per-input px-2 py-1.5 overrides the global tokenized input padding (globals.css:342), so these controls are visibly shorter than every other input in the admin and the form rhythm breaks across pages.
No cross-field validation: dateFrom later than dateTo, or minAmount above maxAmount, is accepted and silently returns nothing.

All 14 status colours are raw Tailwind default-palette classes, not globals.css tokens, and they are all light-mode 100/800 pairs applied inside a dark-default admin — they neither match the marigold/teal/rose editorial system nor respond to the theme switch.

Eight of the fourteen order statuses are absent from CATALOG_STATUSES, so they bypass translation and render their raw English enum identifier (e.g. AWAITING_PRICE_APPROVAL, NO_SHOW_REDISPATCH) to a Hindi-first operator.

The colour system is not injective: COMPLETED and CLOSED share bg-green-100; UNFULFILLED, CUSTOMER_CANCELLED and CANCELLED all share bg-red-100; IN_PROGRESS and NO_SHOW_REDISPATCH share bg-orange-100 — operationally distinct states are visually identical.

CATALOG_STATUSES lists statuses (NEW, ACCEPTED, ARRIVED, REFUNDED) that do not exist in STATUS_STYLES, so if any of them ever reach the badge the className interpolates `undefined` and the pill renders with no background at all.

Status is conveyed by colour + text only — no semantic icon, which the locked baseline requires for mixed-literacy users (icon + text, never icon alone implies text should not be alone either where an icon adds redundancy).

All 14 status option labels render the raw English enum in monospace as the user-facing label AND as the checkbox aria-label, so the primary orders filter is entirely untranslated in a Hindi-default product.
The popover has no Escape-key dismissal and no focus containment — only a mousedown click-outside listener — so it is a keyboard trap-adjacent control that cannot be closed without a mouse.

Clear immediately commits (calls onChange([]) and closes) while Apply is required to commit checkbox edits — two different commit models in the same footer, so a user who unchecks boxes and clicks Clear loses the distinction.
Apply, the primary commit control, is roughly a 24px-tall text-xs button in the popover footer, smaller than the checkbox rows above it.
The popover opens with no motion despite globals.css defining --duration-fast/--ease-out for exactly this.
role="dialog" is applied to a non-modal filter popover, which misrepresents it to assistive tech and also triggers the nested-dialog ESC guard in OrderSlideOver (line 54) if both are ever open.

Customer phone numbers render unmasked in the list view for every operator role, with no masking, no reveal-on-demand, and no capability gate — a PII exposure on the densest, most-shoulder-surfed screen.
Phone is neither a tel: link nor copyable — an ops console whose core job is calling customers offers no click-to-call.
The name line has no truncate/max-width, so long Hindi names expand the column rather than ellipsing (contrast with ComplaintCard.tsx:68 which does truncate).

The 'unassigned' state — the single most action-demanding value in a dispatch table — is rendered in the lowest-contrast muted italic with no icon, no chip, and no colour, so it recedes instead of demanding attention.
The technician ID is silently truncated to 12 characters with no title/tooltip, so the operator cannot read or copy the full ID from the list.
When a technician has an ID but no name, the cell shows only a mono ID fragment — no fallback label, no lookup affordance.

All six override actions — including Refund, Waive fee and force-Complete — share one identical neutral gray button style with no destructive colour, no icon, and no visual weighting, so an irreversible financial action looks exactly like 'add note'.

The refund flow captures no amount and displays no amount — refundOrder is called with only a reason string, so the operator confirms a refund without the sum ever appearing in the confirmation surface.

Reason capture is a free-text textarea with only a minimum-length check (default 5 characters, ConfirmModal.tsx:32/49) — there is no structured reason CODE, no enum, and no category, so the audit trail for financial overrides is unstructured prose.
No action in the panel is reversible or presented as reversible — there is no undo, no pending/void window, and no 'this cannot be undone' warning on refund, waive-fee or force-complete.

Every failure across six different operations collapses to one generic translated message with the real error discarded by an argument-less catch, so an operator cannot distinguish a permission rejection from a network failure from a business-rule violation.

The escalation priority select is permanently visible above the button grid even though it configures only one of the six actions, and it is styled as a ~20px text-xs control — the smallest target in the panel governs how severe an escalation is.

Lacking financial capability silently removes the Refund and Waive-fee buttons with no disabled state or explanation, so the UI misrepresents the available action set rather than communicating a permission boundary.
The six trigger buttons are never disabled while an action is in flight — `loading` is only forwarded to the modal — so a modal-adjacent double-trigger path is not guarded at the panel level.
The technician candidate option label is a hardcoded Latin template with an English 'km' unit, so the reassign picker is untranslated for a Hindi operator.
